chapter: Long Island years and Battle's estate
title: How hard Battle's records would be to sell
summary: They discuss needing a hit, selling a catalog in a lump, retaining percentage rights, and producers not wanting another name on the label.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: I mean, there was a guy in Switzerland, Johnny Simmon -- you know him, don't you?
Yeah.
Well, I mean, he was -- I suppose he took back 50 or 100 each of the records and he sold them, but that was, you know, (inaudible).
See, you got to have hits, though. You got to get a hit song on one.
Sure, to establish a label.
If you can't sit down and create a hit, just music -- a lot of guys can write a great arrangement, you

know, and good songs, but you've got to -- I don't know, you know -- you got to get a band that can -- you got to perform a miracle. Basie made a good thing out of "Shiny Stockings" and stuff like that. (Inaudible) been recorded with Basie's band, too. You never know. Some other bands (inaudible) put on the market might, you know. You can't tell. But you got to sit down and be able to really create something new and different like Herb ________ did with his little outfit. Not him, not that style, but he did reach out and do something. He got over them, because nobody had nothing else like it.

Well, the stuff he's got, just from my experience of it, would not be too easy to sell. You know, I mean, you ________ Lloyd Phillips record, for instance, is quite nice, but you'd have a job selling it. The record with all those tenors.
The name wouldn't carry it, would it?
Hm?
The name wouldn't make it go.
No, and that record --
No matter how good it is, it still ain't -- even if the public accepts it, you can't get it across to the man to promote it. He won't.
Well, that's what I mean. I mean, I could see where you could find somebody and you could sell all those things (inaudible). Well, I mean, right now, I've got
about ten albums that I know (inaudible) Columbia in England. But they've never been issued here. For instance, there's one with Emmett Berry, Paul Gonsalves --
Yeah, well, that --
-- and people like that.
(Inaudible) musician.

Without hearing the rest of that material, the best thing to do would be to put it into sort of some shape on tape and sell it in a lump for, you know -- it's no good sticking out for what it's truly worth.
(Inaudible) some money, profit. Small profit.
Get some money.
And if you can hang on to the rights of it, (inaudible) percentage, piece of percentage of it, then if it takes off, you got a percentage of it. That's what the big publishers done (inaudible).

With the idea that you could come and say, 'Well, I want 5,000 ______ for this.' You'd never get it, you know (inaudible). (Inaudible) six pieces on each one and he did three sessions and I forget what -- this is several years ago -- I forget what he asked for them, but he was on the phone to me one night and I said, 'Barney, I have to tell you the truth. You'll never get it.' And his wife got on the phone to me and said, 'What do you mean, he'll never get
it? Well, who are you to tell him?" "Well," I said, "I'm just telling him what I think. She was very annoyed with me.
Did he ever get it?

: No, he never sold them. It's not easy because these producers with these record companies are looking to get their name on the record as a producer and are not interested in seeing, "Produced by Eddie Battle" on the label (inaudible).
